title: Romans
subtitle: God's righteousness for Jew and Gentile alike
lead: Romans is the longest of Paul's letters and a letter that has repeatedly reshaped Christian teaching. Paul wrote it from Corinth in the winter of about AD 56–57 to the house churches of Rome, a city he had never visited, and it is the fullest surviving statement of his teaching. Its theme is stated in 1:16–17: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, because in it God's righteousness is revealed. Its argument runs from the world's guilt (1:18–3:20), through righteousness by faith (3:21–4:25) and life in Christ and the Spirit (5–8), to the place of Israel (9–11) and the shape of the Christian community (12–15).

Romans is also a letter written to real people. The Roman believers were Jews and Gentiles, meeting in several house groups, and they had lived through the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius and the return that followed. Paul had friends among them, among them Prisca and Aquila (16:3), and he wanted their help for a mission to Spain (15:24). Some of the questions the letter answers are about how a sinner is right with God. Many are about how Jew and Gentile belong together in the family of Abraham. This site presents the readings of both questions side by side: the Reformation and Catholic readings of justification, the Orthodox reading of salvation as healing, the New Perspective, and the Jewish readings of Paul as a Jew.
facts: Paul, undisputed by almost every scholar. The letter was written down by a scribe, Tertius, who greets the readers himself (16:22).
Winter of about AD 56–57 (some say 55 or 58), during the three months Paul spent in Greece (Acts 20:2–3), just before he took the collection to Jerusalem (15:25–31).
Corinth: Paul commends Phoebe of Cenchreae, Corinth's harbor (16:1), and sends greetings from Gaius, his host (16:23), and Erastus, the city treasurer (16:23).
A letter in the ancient style, with a long argument that uses the diatribe, a teacher's lecture with an imagined partner who asks questions and is answered ("What shall we say? By no means!").
Greek, with many quotations from the Old Testament, mostly in the Greek translation (the Septuagint).
authorship: Romans is one of the seven letters almost all scholars accept as Paul's own (with 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon). Almost every critic, even those who reject other letters, accepts Romans; only a few radical critics of the 19th century (Bruno Bauer and the Dutch Radical school) denied it.

In 16:22 Tertius adds his own greeting, "I, Tertius, who wrote this letter." Ancient letter writers often dictated to a secretary (Cicero's Tiro). Scholars debate how much freedom a secretary had; Romans' style is Paul's.

Most scholars accept chapter 16 as part of the letter to Rome (Gamble, Lampe, Dunn, Moo). A minority argue it was a note commending Phoebe, sent to Ephesus with a copy of the letter, because it greets so many people for a church Paul had not seen, and Prisca and Aquila were last known in Ephesus (T. W. Manson, Käsemann). Another view: Paul knew many Romans because Rome was a city to which people came from everywhere, and his greetings are a way of building trust.

A few scholars think parts were added later: 2:16 (Bultmann), 13:1–7 (O'Neill), 16:17–20, and the closing doxology 16:25–27. For 2:16, 13:1–7 and 16:17–20, most scholars defend the verses as Paul's. For the doxology 16:25–27, scholars are divided, and many think it was added after Paul, since its position varies in the manuscripts; others defend it as Paul's (Cranfield, Moo). The textual note below gives the manuscript evidence.

audience.to: The Christians in Rome, "all God's loved ones in Rome, called to be saints" (1:7): Jewish and Gentile believers who met in at least five house groups (16:5, 10, 11, 14, 15), in a city of perhaps a million people. No apostle had founded the church, and Paul had not visited it (1:10–13; 15:22–24). He knew some of its members: Prisca and Aquila, who had been expelled from Rome by Claudius, had worked with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus (Acts 18:2–3, 18; 1 Corinthians 16:19) and were now back in Rome with a church in their house (16:3–5). The church was probably begun by Jews and Jewish Christians who had heard the good news in the synagogues, and its Gentile members had come in through them.
audience.why: Paul writes to prepare for his visit and for a new mission. He is about to take the collection from the Gentile churches to Jerusalem and expects trouble (15:30–31); he wants Rome to pray for him and then to send him on to Spain (15:24, 28). He also knows that the Roman believers are not at ease with each other. The expulsion of Jews under Claudius (about AD 49) and their return after 54 probably upset the balance between Jewish and Gentile Christians, on one common reconstruction; "the weak" and "the strong" (14:1–15:13) suggest tensions over food laws and special days. A rumor was also going around that Paul taught people to ignore the law (3:8). So he sets out his gospel at length, and with the question that mattered in Rome: how can the Jew and the Gentile belong to one people of God? Knowing this audience changes how the letter reads. The long arguments about the law, circumcision and Abraham are as much about the relations of two groups in a Roman congregation as about an individual's guilt, though the letter has both.
views: Paul's remark that he writes "to you Gentiles" (11:13) and his statement of his Gentile mission (1:5–6, 13; 15:15–16) suggest that the majority of readers were Gentiles, with a Jewish minority (Moo, Fitzmyer, Lampe).
A mixed church of Jewish background
The letter's concern with the law, Abraham and Israel suggests Gentile believers who had learned their faith from Jewish teachers and a church led by Jews (Dunn, Wright).

Several house groups with different customs: some, mainly Jewish, kept food laws and special days ("the weak"); others, mainly Gentile, did not ("the strong"). Paul's letter is aimed at their mutual contempt (Wedderburn, Wright, Nanos).

outline: The thesis: the good news reveals God's righteousness
Sin: all humanity, Gentile and Jew, is under sin
Righteousness: God's righteousness through faith, shown in Christ and in Abraham
Life: peace, Adam and Christ, freedom from sin and law, the Spirit and the hope of glory
Israel: God's promises, the remnant, the olive tree and "all Israel"
Living: the body of Christ, love, the authorities, the weak and the strong
Paul's plans and mission, greetings, and the closing doxology

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Romans against Rome in the 50s: the house churches, the Jewish community and Claudius' expulsion (about AD 49), Paul writing from Corinth with the collection for Jerusalem in hand, Roman law, patronage, slavery and adoption, taxes and the names of chapter 16 in inscriptions. Used by historians from Peter Lampe to Robert Jewett.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made and why: the purpose of Romans (the "Romans debate"), Tertius the scribe, the diatribe style, whether chapter 16 went to Rome or Ephesus, the position of the doxology (16:25–27), the proposed interpolations (2:16; 13:1–7; 16:17–20), and the manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Claromontanus, Boernerianus).

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's design: the salutation (1:1–7), the thesis (1:16–17) built on Habakkuk 2:4, the four movements, the diatribe and its "What shall we say? By no means!", the Adam and Christ contrast, Paul's use of Scripture, and the "obedience of faith" framing 1:5 and 16:26.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jew who wrote to Gentiles: Stendahl's "Paul among Jews and Gentiles," the New Perspective (Sanders, Dunn, Wright), the "Paul within Judaism" readings (Nanos, Gager, Fredriksen, Campbell, Boyarin), "works of the law," the Jew's advantage, Israel in chapters 9–11 and the misuse of Romans against Jews. Includes Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine and Jon Levenson.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows how the churches have read Romans: Origen and Chrysostom, Augustine against Pelagius, Pelagius' own commentary, Aquinas, Luther's preface, Melanchthon and Calvin, Wesley, Barth, Orthodox readings (Cyril of Alexandria, Theophylact, theosis), and Catholic teaching (Trent session 6, the 1999 Joint Declaration).

sections.b:
Romans is a letter, not a textbook. Paul argues, but he argues with people in mind: a Jewish teacher who is proud of the law, a Gentile who looks down on Jews, a weak believer and a strong one. Read it with the imagined questions in mind: what advantage the Jew has (3:1), whether believers should continue in sin (6:1), whether the law is sin (7:7), and whether God has rejected his people (11:1). Each "By no means!" opens a new stage in the argument.

Key words are given the same English each time in this Plain: righteousness (dikaiosyne), justify (dikaioo), faith (pistis), grace (charis), law (nomos), sin (hamartia), flesh (sarx), anger (orge) and reckon (logizomai). A reader who follows them from chapter to chapter sees the pattern that translations with many synonyms hide. The notes give the other renderings and the places where they matter.

sections.h: Why Paul wrote: the Romans debate
sections.b:
Why did Paul write the most thorough of his letters to a church he did not know? Since the 1970s scholars have called this "the Romans debate." The leading answers:

  • A summary of his gospel for a church that might meet him as a stranger (Günther Bornkamm's "last will and testament").
  • Support for Spain. He needs the Roman house churches to back his mission to the west, and he must first show they can trust his teaching (Robert Jewett).
  • Unity of Jews and Gentiles in Rome. The Jewish and Gentile believers, divided after Claudius' edict and the return of the exiles, must accept each other, and the long argument of 1–11 prepares the practical appeal of 14–15 (A. J. M. Wedderburn, Stanley Stowers, N. T. Wright).
  • A defense before Jerusalem. He is rehearsing the arguments he must give to Jewish Christians when he delivers the collection (Jacob Jervell).

Most scholars combine two or three. Karl Donfried's collection The Romans Debate gathers the main papers.

sections.h: The church in Rome and the edict of Claudius
sections.b:
The Roman historian Suetonius says that the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly making disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus (Claudius 25.4). Many scholars read "Chrestus" as a garbling of "Christ" and see here a quarrel in the synagogues over Jesus; the identification is debated, and a man named Chrestus is possible. Acts 18:2 says that Aquila and Priscilla "had just come from Italy, since Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome." The date is debated: AD 41 (according to Cassius Dio, who says Claudius forbade Jewish assemblies but did not expel them) or about AD 49 (the date Orosius gives, citing Josephus, whom we do not have on this point).

When Claudius died in 54, those who had been expelled began to return. On one reconstruction (Wedderburn and others), Gentile Christians had led the house churches in the interval, and when Prisca and Aquila were back (16:3), the leadership and customs of the Roman house churches might have been in question. This history is, on that view, the background of the tension between "the weak" and "the strong" in 14:1–15:13, and it helps explain why Paul writes about Jews and Gentiles at such length.

PartPassageWhat Paul argues
Sin1:18–3:20Gentiles and Jews alike are under sin. God's anger is revealed against the nations (1:18–32); the judge who judges is judged by the same standard (2:1–16); the one who calls himself a Jew has the law but breaks it (2:17–29); Israel's advantage is real but gives no exemption (3:1–8); the Scriptures say all are under sin (3:9–20).
Righteousness3:21–4:25God's righteousness has been made plain in Christ, received by faith by Jew and Gentile alike (3:21–31). Abraham is the proof: reckoned righteous by faith before circumcision, and father of all who believe (4).
Life5–8Peace with God and hope (5:1–11); Adam and Christ (5:12–21); freedom from sin's rule, from the law and from death by union with Christ (6–7); the Spirit, adoption, the groaning creation and the love from which nothing can separate us (8).
Israel9–11Has God's word failed? The promises, the election of Jacob, the stumbling stone, the remnant, the olive tree, the mystery, and the doxology (11:33–36).
Living12:1–15:13The living sacrifice and the body; love, enemies and the authorities; love fulfills the law; the weak and the strong; Christ the servant of Jews and Gentiles.
Plans and greetings15:14–16:27Paul's ministry, the collection for Jerusalem, the mission to Spain; Phoebe and the long list of greetings; the closing doxology.

Paul reads Scripture in Greek, mostly the Septuagint, and sometimes his Greek differs from the Hebrew that this site translates. Richard Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul) argues that Paul's quotations carry their whole context with them: to hear Habakkuk 2:4, one must hear Habakkuk's question about God's justice. Paul's "the Lord" in 10:13, which translates the divine name in Joel 2:32 and is applied to Jesus, is a note in the part for chapters 9–11.

The oldest large copy is the papyrus P46 (dated from the late 100s to the mid 200s; about AD 200 is the usual figure), but its surviving leaves begin at 5:17. For chapters 1–4 the oldest witnesses are fragments such as the third-century papyrus P40. Sinaiticus (01) and Vaticanus (03) are from the 300s, with Alexandrinus (02) and Ephraemi (04) from the 400s; Claromontanus (06) and Boernerianus (012) are Greek-Latin manuscripts of the 500s and 800s that preserve an earlier Western text. The Editio Critica Maior does not yet cover Romans. This Plain follows the SBL Greek New Testament and checks it against NA28 and the Tyndale House text; each variant that changes the English has its own entry.

The shorter Romans. Several features suggest the letter circulated in different forms. A few witnesses omit "in Rome" in 1:7 and 1:15 (Boernerianus and a few others; see the entries). The closing doxology (16:25–27) stands in different places. As reported in Metzger's commentary and the NA28 apparatus, it comes after 14:23 in the Byzantine majority and in L and Ψ; after 16:23 in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi and Claromontanus; after 15:33 in P46; in both places in Alexandrinus and a few others; and not at all in Augiensis (F) and Boernerianus (G), where G leaves a blank space. The verse numbers at the end of the letter vary by edition. Origen, as translated by Rufinus, reports that Marcion cut the letter from 14:23 to the end; whether Marcion cut the text or simply did not have it is debated (Gamble). Scholars debate what lies behind this: a short form for general reading (Harry Gamble), the work of later editors, or ordinary scribal accident. Gamble argues that chapter 16 belonged to the letter from the start.

The omitted verse. 16:24, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all," is in the Byzantine text but not in the oldest manuscripts; the Plain marks it as the policy of this site requires.

Early centuries. Origen wrote the first great commentary (the surviving text is Rufinus' shortened Latin). Chrysostom preached 32 homilies on Romans. Pelagius wrote a commentary about AD 405–410 that denied inherited guilt, and Augustine answered him; the fight made 5:12 and chapter 7 central to Western teaching on sin and grace. The Orthodox East kept Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria and Theophylact of Ohrid as its guides and spoke of salvation as healing and sharing in God's life.

Conversions. Augustine (Confessions 8.12) heard a child's voice in a Milan garden saying "Take and read" (tolle lege), opened Romans and read 13:13–14. Luther, in the preface to his Latin works (1545), told how in the tower of the Wittenberg monastery he came to see that "the righteousness of God" (1:17) is a gift. On 24 May 1738 at a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London, John Wesley felt his heart "strangely warmed" while someone read Luther's preface to Romans. Karl Barth's Römerbrief (1919; second edition 1922) shook liberal theology and brought a new reading of the letter to the 20th century.

Catholic and Protestant. Aquinas lectured on Romans; Luther and Melanchthon wrote on it; Calvin's commentary (1540) was the first of his New Testament commentaries; the Council of Trent's decree on justification (1547) answered Luther; and in 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church issued a Joint Declaration saying their remaining differences over justification did not warrant mutual condemnation.

Romans has been used against Jews and for them. Some Christians have read 2:28–29 and chapters 9–11 to say that the church replaced Israel (supersessionism). Others, after the Holocaust, have read the same chapters to say the opposite: that God has not rejected his people (11:1) and that the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29), words cited in Nostra Aetate 4.

Scholars have also asked whether the picture of Paul as a critic of Judaism is right. Krister Stendahl argued that Paul was not troubled by guilt about the law but concerned with how Gentiles could be included. E. P. Sanders argued that Judaism of the time was a religion of covenant and grace, a picture that many scholars have accepted and that others (Gathercole, Carson, and, with refinements, Barclay) say does not fit every Jewish text. James Dunn and N. T. Wright (the "New Perspective") read "works of the law" as the markers of Jewish identity. Mark Nanos and Paula Fredriksen (the "Paul within Judaism" readings) go further and say Paul never left Judaism and wrote to Gentiles, not Jews; Pamela Eisenbaum stresses how Jewish Paul was; Lloyd Gaston and John Gager argue that Paul spoke of different ways for Jews and for Gentiles. Daniel Boyarin argues that Paul was a Jew with a Platonizing view of flesh and spirit. Other scholars hold the traditional reading, in which Paul does criticize a legalistic strand of Judaism. The notes mark the debated points.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Romans follows the shape of the Exodus
spec.body: The plot of Romans may be a retelling of the Exodus. Humanity is in bondage under sin (1:18–3:20, 6:16–20). God redeems by a price (the redemption in Christ Jesus, 3:24), as at the Passover, and the blood of a sacrifice is shown (3:25). Believers pass through the water into new life (6:3–4, baptism as the crossing). They meet the law as at Sinai (7) and then walk under the guidance of the Spirit as a people in the wilderness (8:14, those led by the Spirit of God), groaning for the inheritance (8:17–25). The "firstfruits" (8:23) and the adoption (8:15) recall Israel as God's firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). The letter would then tell, in order, how God makes a new Israel of Jew and Gentile together out of a world held in slavery. This is my reading of the plan; N. T. Wright, Sylvia Keesmaat and Richard Hays have each seen parts of the pattern (Wright reads the letter's central movement as a new exodus; Keesmaat has done the same for chapter 8), but none that I know of has argued it as the plot of the whole letter, chapters 1–16.
spec.refs: Exodus 4:22; Exodus 12:1–14; Exodus 14:21–31; Romans 3:24–25; Romans 6:3–4; Romans 8:14–23

prompts: Paul dictates to Tertius at Corinth

A scribe's room in a harbor city: Paul, a man with a lined, serious face (no description of his looks survives from his own time), in a plain tunic and cloak, walks the floor as he speaks, one hand raised; Tertius sits at a low table with a reed pen and a long papyrus sheet partly written in Greek; an oil lamp burns; through a window open to the sea are the masts of ships at Cenchreae; scrolls lie in a basket on the floor.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with ancient manuscript borders, cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor washes; ink lines wobble a little, edges fade into rough parchment; no hard rectangular frame.

The courtyard of a Roman apartment block at dusk: about thirty people, Jews in fringed cloaks and Gentiles in tunics and togas, share a meal on mats and low couches; a woman (Prisca) hands bread to a man (Aquila) at the center; a scroll is being unrolled and read by lamplight; across the courtyard a smaller group sits apart eating different food, looking over; children play near a small fountain.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with ancient manuscript borders, cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor washes; soft edges, no hard rectangle.

A night plain with a single tent; Abraham, an old man with a long white beard, stands outside with his head thrown back and his arms open, the sky a swarm of hand-drawn stars; beside him, small and faint, the shapes of many different peoples in different clothing walk toward him over the dunes in the distance; a few figures hold scrolls; Sarah looks out from the tent flap.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with cave-painting stars, ancient manuscript borders and loose modern ink; soft edges, no hard rectangle.

The gold lid of the ark of the covenant with two winged cherubim facing each other, wings touching above it; a ray of soft light falls on the lid, and a bowl of blood rests before it; behind the veil, the shape of a single wooden cross is just visible as a pale watermark in the parchment; the high priest's hands, in blue and gold, rest on the lid.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment in the manner of an illuminated manuscript, with cave-painting red ochre, hieroglyph-like borders and modern ink wash; soft edges, no hard rectangle.

traditions.q: What is Romans mainly about, and how have the churches read it?
views: Romans is the apostle's teaching on grace, faith and the new life. The Council of Trent (session 6) cites it for justification as the sanctification and renewal of the inner person, by grace and faith working through love; the Church reads its teaching on baptism, sin and the Spirit with the rest of Scripture and tradition. In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans issued a Joint Declaration on justification.

The Orthodox read Romans through Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria and Theophylact, and they stress that sin and death are healed by union with Christ and the Spirit (theosis). Romans is not read mainly as a courtroom drama, and the Western debates about imputation are not part of the Orthodox tradition.

Luther's preface (1522) calls Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the purest gospel." The letter's center is justification by faith alone, and the law's work is to show sin (3:20; 7:7). Melanchthon's first theology, the Loci Communes (1521), was an outline of Romans.

Calvin's dedication of his commentary (1540) says that anyone who understands Romans has a way into the whole of Scripture. The Reformed churches read the letter as a statement of grace and of Christ's righteousness counted to the believer (Westminster Confession 11), and chapters 8–9 as the chief text on election (Westminster Confession 3).

The Thirty-Nine Articles draw the teaching of the letter into one statement: we are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of Christ, by faith (Article 11), and good works are the fruit of faith (Article 12).
Baptists read Romans through the Second London Confession, which teaches that God justifies by counting Christ's obedience to believers, with faith as the instrument (chapter 11).

Wesley's heart was "strangely warmed" as Luther's preface to Romans was read at Aldersgate Street (1738). Methodists read Romans as a letter of free grace, the witness of the Spirit (8:16) and holiness, set against Calvin's reading of election.

A full-length Reformed commentary, careful about the Greek and the churches' history of reading the letter.

A clear evangelical commentary that weighs the New Perspective and mostly keeps the traditional reading.

The New Perspective's chief commentary, with much on Paul and Judaism.

A Catholic commentary with careful notes on the language and the history of interpretation.

The great modern history and rhetoric commentary: the house churches, honor and shame, and the mission to Spain.

A narrative, covenant reading of the whole, with a lively style.

A German Lutheran commentary that reads "the righteousness of God" as God's saving power.
